borders.before: the lecturer's introduction, course background, and lecture learning objectives
borders.after: the core definition of cancer as a genetic, evolutionary disease and the role of the microenvironment
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 1 is opening framing and orientation, whereas subtopic 2 begins substantive teaching on the nature and causes of cancer.
borders.caseForMoving: There is no reasonable intermediate position because subtopic 1 is purely introductory and subtopic 2 immediately begins the core lecture content.
borders.caseForRemoving: Combining introductory lecture framing with the substantive explanation of cancer biology would ignore the clear boundary between course admin and content.

borders.before: the overarching debate on cancer etiology, bad luck, and epidemiological geographic variation
borders.after: specific biological and infectious agents that drive carcinogenesis, starting with pathogens like H. pylori and EBV
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 7 marks the shift from high-level epidemiological and conceptual discussions of cancer causation to detailed molecular and cellular mechanisms of specific carcinogens.
borders.caseForMoving: Moving the border to subtopic 8 would orphan the general introduction to infectious agents in subtopic 7, while moving it earlier to subtopic 6 would place broad geographical epidemiology into the specific mechanistic section.
borders.caseForRemoving: Merging high-level etiology and population epidemiology with detailed molecular pathways would create an overly broad topic spanning distinct pedagogical questions.

borders.before: the summary of direct and indirect mechanisms of DNA damage and tumor promotion
borders.after: high-throughput DNA sequencing and the identification of mutational signatures associated with specific carcinogens
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 18 turns to the methodological question of how carcinogenicity is proven and detected experimentally and genomically, ending the preceding discussion on biological mechanisms.
borders.caseForMoving: Moving the border before subtopic 17 would incorrectly separate a summary from the mechanisms it recaps, while moving it after subtopic 18 would split mutational signature analysis from the rest of the testing methodologies.
borders.caseForRemoving: Merging the biological mechanisms of carcinogenesis with the experimental and epidemiological methodologies used to prove them would blur two distinct learning objectives.

borders.before: in vitro Ames test mutagenicity assays and their limitations regarding tumor microenvironments
borders.after: overarching conclusions on daily risk-benefit decisions regarding carcinogen exposure and final sign-off
borders.caseForKeeping: Subtopic 22 provides closing framing, synthesizing personal and regulatory risk-benefit choices and wrapping up the lecture.
borders.caseForMoving: Moving the border to subtopic 21 would incorporate specific technical details of the Ames test into the lecture closing.
borders.caseForRemoving: Merging the lecture's concluding remarks with the technical evaluation of toxicological assays violates the distinction between closing framing and substantive content.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 2 and 3 discuss theoretical frameworks of cancer as a genetic and evolutionary process driven by intrinsic factors, while subtopics 4 to 6 focus on environmental exposures, public perception of risk, and global epidemiological studies.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 2 to 6 form a single conceptual introduction to cancer etiology, establishing the interplay between intrinsic bad luck, inherited genetic predisposition, and environmental risk factors.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopics 7 to 13 examine direct mutagens and DNA-damaging agents (biological, chemical, and physical), whereas subtopics 14 to 17 address non-mutagenic tumor promotion, chronic inflammation, and developmental stage susceptibility.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 7 to 17 form a continuous, cohesive examination of the cellular and molecular mechanisms of carcinogenesis, integrating both direct initiating mutations and indirect promotional pathways.

insides.caseForDividing: Subtopic 18 focuses on modern genomic sequencing and mutational signatures, whereas subtopics 19 to 21 focus on traditional epidemiological biobanks, in vivo animal toxicology, and in vitro Ames testing.
insides.caseForKeepingWhole: Subtopics 18 to 21 collectively answer the single overarching question of what experimental and epidemiological tools are used to establish and prove carcinogenicity.

topics.label: Lecture introduction and learning objectives
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic introduces the lecturer, the cancer lecture series, and the key learning outcomes regarding environmental exposures, mechanisms, and methodologies.

topics.label: Cancer etiology: bad luck, genetics, and environmental exposure
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explore the foundational causes of cancer by examining the balance between endogenous random mutations, genetic predispositions, and environmental exposures through conceptual models and epidemiological data.

topics.label: Mechanisms of chemical, physical, and biological carcinogenesis
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics detail the molecular and cellular mechanisms through which infectious pathogens, chemical mutagens, radiation, and non-mutagenic promoters initiate and drive tumor development.

topics.label: Methodologies for identifying and proving carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics survey the genomic, epidemiological, animal, and in vitro experimental methodologies used to identify carcinogen exposure and prove carcinogenic potential.

topics.label: Conclusion and risk-benefit analysis
topics.groupedBecause: This subtopic concludes the lecture with an overarching synthesis of daily risk-benefit evaluations regarding carcinogen exposure and final remarks.
